claim: Cytochromes c are ubiquitous heme proteins in mitochondria and bacteria.
source: Cytochromes c are ubiquitous heme proteins in mitochondria and bacteria, all possessing a CXXCH (CysXxxXxxCysHis) motif with covalently attached heme.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about cytochromes c.

claim: All cytochromes c possess a CXXCH (CysXxxXxxCysHis) motif with covalently attached heme.
source: Cytochromes c are ubiquitous heme proteins in mitochondria and bacteria, all possessing a CXXCH (CysXxxXxxCysHis) motif with covalently attached heme.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a defining characteristic of cytochromes c.

claim: This is the first in vitro reconstitution of cytochrome c biogenesis using purified mitochondrial (HCCS) and bacterial (CcsBA) cytochrome c synthases.
source: We describe the first in vitro reconstitution of cytochrome c biogenesis using purified mitochondrial (HCCS) and bacterial (CcsBA) cytochrome c synthases.
evidence: This is a primary claim stated in the abstract describing the novelty of the work.

claim: For HCCS, a minimal 16-mer peptide is required, comprised of CXXCH and adjacent alpha helix 1.
source: For HCCS, a minimal 16-mer peptide is required, comprised of CXXCH and adjacent alpha helix 1, yet neither thiol is critical for recognition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data with peptides shown in Figure 3.

claim: For HCCS, neither thiol is critical for recognition.
source: For HCCS, a minimal 16-mer peptide is required, comprised of CXXCH and adjacent alpha helix 1, yet neither thiol is critical for recognition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cysteine substitution experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: For bacterial CcsBA, both thiols and histidine are required for recognition.
source: For bacterial CcsBA, both thiols and histidine are required, but not alpha helix 1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by peptide experiments shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: For bacterial CcsBA, alpha helix 1 is not required for recognition.
source: For bacterial CcsBA, both thiols and histidine are required, but not alpha helix 1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing CcsBA attaches heme to 11-mer peptide lacking alpha helix 1 (Figure 7).

claim: Heme attached peptide analogs are not released from the HCCS active site.
source: Heme attached peptide analogs are not released from the HCCS active site; thus, folding is important in the release mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by release assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Folding is important in the release mechanism of cytochrome c from HCCS.
source: Heme attached peptide analogs are not released from the HCCS active site; thus, folding is important in the release mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an inference from the observation that peptides are not released while full-length cyt c is released.

claim: Peptide analogs behave as inhibitors of cytochrome c biogenesis.
source: Peptide analogs behave as inhibitors of cytochrome c biogenesis, paving the way for targeted control.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by inhibition assay data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The structure of cytochrome c has been known for over half a century.
source: The structure of cytochrome c (cyt c), as well as its key function in electron transport for aerobic respiration, have been known for over half a century (Dickerson et al., 1971; Ernster and Schatz, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to historical literature.

claim: The key function of cytochrome c in electron transport for aerobic respiration has been known for over half a century.
source: The structure of cytochrome c (cyt c), as well as its key function in electron transport for aerobic respiration, have been known for over half a century (Dickerson et al., 1971; Ernster and Schatz, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to historical literature.

claim: Extracellular multiheme nanowires are comprised of many c-type hemes.
source: Scores of newly discovered and extraordinary electron transport chains with unique cyt c proteins in bacteria are now known, such as extracellular multiheme nanowires comprised of many c-type hemes (e.g. Deane, 2019; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to recent literature.

claim: Cytochrome c plays a role in activation of programmed cell death in eukaryotes (apoptosis).
source: In addition to its role in respiration, cyt c is known to play other important functions, such as activation of programmed cell death in eukaryotes (apoptosis) (Ow et al., 2008; Tait and Green, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to literature on apoptosis.

claim: Each c-type heme contains two thioether attachments to a conserved CysXxxXxxCysHis (CXXCH) motif.
source: Regardless of its function, each c-type heme contains two thioether attachments to a conserved CysXxxXxxCysHis (CXXCH) motif, where the histidine acts as an axial ligand to the heme iron in the native cyt c (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b; Dickerson et al., 1971).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to a figure and citation to structural literature.

claim: The histidine of the CXXCH motif acts as an axial ligand to the heme iron in native cytochrome c.
source: Regardless of its function, each c-type heme contains two thioether attachments to a conserved CysXxxXxxCysHis (CXXCH) motif, where the histidine acts as an axial ligand to the heme iron in the native cyt c (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b; Dickerson et al., 1971).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to a figure and citation to structural literature.

claim: The covalently attached heme makes energy conversion proteins particularly stable.
source: It is generally agreed that the covalently attached heme makes these energy conversion proteins particularly stable (e.g. Allen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Recent engineering of novel and stable heme-based catalysts has used c-heme polypeptides produced in vivo.
source: In fact, recent engineering of novel and stable heme-based catalysts has used c-heme polypeptides produced in vivo (Kan et al., 2017; Kan et al., 2016; Watkins et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to recent engineering studies.

claim: In the case of cytochrome c, folding into its native structure occurs after heme attachment.
source: To form c-heme, heme is attached stereochemically to each CXXCH motif and it appears that in the case of cyt c, folding into its native structure occurs after attachment (Kranz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a review article.

claim: Cytochrome c biogenesis requires accessory proteins that are needed to attach the heme group and complete maturation.
source: Cyt c biogenesis requires accessory proteins that are needed to attach the heme group and complete maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the biogenesis process.

claim: Three pathways for cytochrome c biogenesis have been discovered and characterized genetically, called Systems I, II, III.
source: Three pathways have been discovered and characterized genetically, called Systems I, II, III (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c) (reviewed in Kranz et al., 2009; Ferguson et al., 2008; Kranz et al., 1998; Bowman and Bren, 2008; Simon and Hederstedt, 2011; Verissimo and Daldal, 2014; Gabilly and Hamel, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with references to multiple review articles and a figure.

claim: Systems I and II have evolved in bacteria.
source: Systems I and II have evolved in bacteria, while System III is in most mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the distribution of these systems.

claim: System III is in most mitochondria.
source: Systems I and II have evolved in bacteria, while System III is in most mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the distribution of these systems.

claim: Each system possesses a cytochrome c synthase which attaches the two vinyl groups of heme to cysteines of CXXCH.
source: Each system possesses a cyt c synthase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, orange), which attaches the two vinyl groups of heme to cysteines of CXXCH.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to a figure showing the synthases.

claim: The cytochrome c biogenesis process, starting with CXXCH recognition, to heme attachment, to release and final folding, remains largely unknown.
source: However, the cyt c biogenesis process, starting with CXXCH recognition, to heme attachment, to release and final folding, remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction to establish the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: In vivo studies have suggested some requirements for cytochrome c biogenesis but do not examine problems of instability, recognition, release, or folding of the cyt c variants.
source: While in vivo studies have suggested some requirements (Babbitt et al., 2017; Babbitt et al., 2016; Corvest et al., 2010; San Francisco et al., 2013), such cyt c genetic studies do not examine problems of instability, recognition, release, or folding of the cyt c variants.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous in vivo studies and their limitations.

claim: Direct testing of substrates without limitations of in vivo studies awaited the development of in vitro reconstitution.
source: Direct testing of substrates without these limitations awaited the development of in vitro reconstitution.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction to justify the need for the in vitro approach.

claim: The mitochondrial System III is composed of a cytochrome c synthase called HCCS (holocytochrome c synthase) in the intermembrane space.
source: The mitochondrial System III is composed of a cyt c synthase called HCCS (holocyt c synthase) in the intermembrane space (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, Pollock et al., 1998; Dumont et al., 1987; Babbitt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to literature and reference to figures.

claim: Bacterial systems are unrelated to HCCS and more complicated, with heme attachment occurring 'outside' the cells.
source: Bacterial systems are unrelated to HCCS and more complicated, heme attachment occurs 'outside' the cells; thus, these pathways export the heme and attach it to secreted, unfolded cyt c.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction to contrast bacterial and mitochondrial systems.

claim: System II is composed of a large integral membrane protein complex called CcsBA.
source: System II is composed of a large integral membrane protein complex called CcsBA (Beckett et al., 2000; Dreyfuss et al., 2003; Xie and Merchant, 1996) (sometimes called ResBC [Ahuja et al., 2009; Le Brun et al., 2000]), which is proposed to both export heme and then attach it to cyt c CXXCH motifs (Feissner et al., 2006; Frawley and Kranz, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to literature on CcsBA.

claim: CcsBA is proposed to both export heme and then attach it to cytochrome c CXXCH motifs.
source: System II is composed of a large integral membrane protein complex called CcsBA (Beckett et al., 2000; Dreyfuss et al., 2003; Xie and Merchant, 1996) (sometimes called ResBC [Ahuja et al., 2009; Le Brun et al., 2000]), which is proposed to both export heme and then attach it to cyt c CXXCH motifs (Feissner et al., 2006; Frawley and Kranz, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to literature proposing this dual function.

claim: Specific factors for thiol reduction of the CXXCH motifs have been proposed.
source: Specific factors for thiol reduction of the CXXCH motifs have also been proposed (Bonnard et al., 2010; Kranz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to literature on thiol reduction factors.

claim: Recombinant human HCCS (GST-tagged) is functional in vivo, attaching heme to co-expressed apocytochrome c in E. coli.
source: Recombinant human HCCS (GST-tagged) is functional in vivo, attaching heme to co-expressed apocyt c (San Francisco et al., 2013) in E. coli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: HCCS co-purifies with heme, which is liganded to His154.
source: We have previously shown that HCCS co-purifies with heme, which is liganded to His154 (San Francisco et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: UV–vis spectra of purified HCCS shows a 423 nm and broad 560 nm absorption, typical of heme proteins.
source: UV–vis spectra of purified HCCS shows a 423 nm and broad 560 nm absorption, typical of heme proteins, while HCCS H154A variant does not bind heme (Figure 1b, −HL).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: HCCS H154A variant does not bind heme.
source: UV–vis spectra of purified HCCS shows a 423 nm and broad 560 nm absorption, typical of heme proteins, while HCCS H154A variant does not bind heme (Figure 1b, −HL).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: A 'heme-loading (HL)' protocol increases the levels of heme bound in HCCS to ~30% occupied above the co-purified levels of endogenous heme (~10% occupied).
source: We developed a 'heme-loading (HL)' protocol to increase the levels of heme bound in HCCS (+HL, ~30% occupied) above the co-purified levels of endogenous heme (−HL, ~10% occupied).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the heme loading method.

claim: Heme loading was shown to depend on the natural His154 ligand.
source: HL was also advantageous since the HL protocol removes excess heme, thus minimizing spectral interference from free heme in reactions. HL was shown to depend on the natural His154 ligand (Figure 1b, +HL black line), and loading was saturated at 2–5 µM heme (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Heme loading was saturated at 2–5 µM heme.
source: HL was also advantageous since the HL protocol removes excess heme, thus minimizing spectral interference from free heme in reactions. HL was shown to depend on the natural His154 ligand (Figure 1b, +HL black line), and loading was saturated at 2–5 µM heme (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Upon incubation for 1 hr in the presence of apocytochrome c and DTT, a sharp 550 nm peak emerged, indicative of a c-type cytochrome.
source: Upon incubation for 1 hr in the presence of apocyt c and dithiothreitol (DTT), a sharp 550 nm peak emerged, indicative of a c-type cytochrome (Figure 1b, red with wt).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The 550 nm peak occurred with wild type HCCS containing endogenous heme (−HL) and in vitro loaded heme (+HL), while HCCS H154A did not produce the 550 nm peak.
source: This occurred with wt HCCS containing endogenous heme (−HL) and in vitro loaded heme (+HL), while HCCS H154A did not produce the 550 nm peak.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the specificity of the reaction.

claim: Reactions with wild type HCCS (−HL and +HL) and apocytochrome c confirmed that heme is covalently attached to cytochrome c (12 kDa) in the 1 hr reaction.
source: Reactions with wt HCCS (−HL and +HL) and apocyt c confirmed that heme is covalently attached to cyt c (12 kDa) in the 1 hr reaction (Figure 1c, lanes 3, 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: No cytochrome c was formed with the HCCS H154A variant.
source: As expected, no cyt c was formed with the HCCS H154A variant (Figure 1c, lanes 5, 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The in vitro synthesized product has two thioether bonds, indicated by a 550 nm peak in pyridine hemochrome spectra.
source: The in vitro synthesized product has two thioether bonds, indicated by a 550 nm peak in pyridine hemochrome spectra (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Synthesis is optimal at 37°C.
source: In vitro reconstitutions were studied for optimal conditions and requirements. Synthesis is optimal at 37°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), required DTT (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), with the cyt c product observed in 10 min (e.g. Figure 1d, lane 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: In vitro synthesis of cytochrome c by HCCS requires DTT.
source: In vitro reconstitutions were studied for optimal conditions and requirements. Synthesis is optimal at 37°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), required DTT (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), with the cyt c product observed in 10 min (e.g. Figure 1d, lane 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The cytochrome c product is observed in 10 min in HCCS in vitro reactions.
source: In vitro reconstitutions were studied for optimal conditions and requirements. Synthesis is optimal at 37°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), required DTT (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), with the cyt c product observed in 10 min (e.g. Figure 1d, lane 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Cytochrome c is formed in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions by HCCS.
source: While cyt c is formed in both aerobic (Figure 1—figure supplement 6) and anaerobic conditions (Figure 1b,c), we decided to use anaerobic conditions for all studies since peptide substrates (below) under aerobic conditions required varying DTT concentrations, likely due to distinct thiol reducing requirements of individual peptides in air.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in multiple figures.

claim: HPLC separation showed that HCCS with the 20mer reaction eluted at the same time as HCCS alone.
source: HPLC separation (Figure 4a) showed that HCCS with the 20mer reaction (blue profile) eluted at the same time as HCCS alone (brown profile), not unexpected since a small 2.8 kD unreleased product would not significantly alter size exclusion properties.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The cytochrome c product is released from the HCCS active site.
source: These results also demonstrate that the cyt c product is released from the HCCS active site since it elutes at the same time as purified cyt c (holocyt c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on HPLC data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The released cytochrome c product has folded properly, forming the Met81 ligand as well as His19.
source: We determined spectrally that the released cyt c has folded properly, forming the Met81 ligand as well as His19 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: The redox potential of the cytochrome c in vitro product is +253 mV, the same as cytochrome c produced in vivo.
source: Redox titrations (Figure 2d) showed that the redox potential of the cyt c in vitro product is the same as cyt c produced in vivo, +253 mV (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: At least 62% of cytochrome c is released from HCCS.
source: Analyses of supernatants (released), washes, and bead-retained material allowed for an estimate that at least 62% of cyt c is released from HCCS (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Cytochrome c synthesized in vitro by HCCS shows an identical CD spectral profile as in vivo synthesized cytochrome c.
source: Cyt c synthesized in vitro by HCCS shows an identical CD spectral profile as in vivo synthesized (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2f.

claim: In vitro reconstitution with purified HCCS results in stereochemical heme attachment, release, and proper folding of cytochrome c.
source: We conclude that in vitro reconstitution with purified HCCS results in stereochemical heme attachment, release, and proper folding of cyt c.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: After 1 hr, reactions showed that the 16mer and 20mer possessed an intense heme-stained peptide of 2.8 kDa, whereas the 11mer did not.
source: After 1 hr, reactions showed that the 16mer (Figure 3b, lane 6) and 20mer (Figure 3b, lane 8) possessed an intense heme-stained peptide of 2.8 kDa, whereas the 11mer did not (Figure 3b, lane 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Spectral analyses showed that the 11mer reaction looked like HCCS alone (no peptide added), whereas the reactions with the 16mer and 20mer showed a 552–553 nm peak.
source: Spectral analyses showed that the 11mer reaction looked like HCCS alone (no peptide added), whereas the reactions with the 16mer and 20mer showed a 552–553 nm peak (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The 56mer was recognized and heme attached by HCCS.
source: To further test CXXCH peptide recognition, we tested a 56mer (with alpha helix 1 and 2 of cyt c) and a 9mer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). While the 56mer was recognized and heme attached, the 9mer was not, consistent with the in vivo results that alpha helix 1 is required for heme attachment (Babbitt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 9mer was not recognized by HCCS.
source: To further test CXXCH peptide recognition, we tested a 56mer (with alpha helix 1 and 2 of cyt c) and a 9mer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). While the 56mer was recognized and heme attached, the 9mer was not, consistent with the in vivo results that alpha helix 1 is required for heme attachment (Babbitt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alpha helix 1 is necessary and sufficient for recognition and attachment to the adjacent CXXCH motif by HCCS.
source: We conclude that alpha helix 1 is necessary and sufficient for recognition and attachment to the adjacent CXXCH motif.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on peptide experiments.

claim: Folding of cytochrome c is required for optimal release from the HCCS active site.
source: Our findings suggest that folding of cyt c is required for optimal release from the HCCS active site (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on release assay data.

claim: Both the purified GST-CcsBA and metal-affinity purified CcsBA:His, both with endogenous heme, were active for heme attachment to apocytochrome c in vitro.
source: Using the anaerobic in vitro reconstitution conditions described above for HCCS, both the purified GST-CcsBA and metal-affinity purified CcsBA:His, both with endogenous heme, were active for heme attachment to apocyt c in vitro (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The GST:CcsBA P-His variant did not attach heme to apocytochrome c in vitro.
source: Importantly, the GST:CcsBA P-His variant did not attach heme to apocyt c in vitro (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Within 1–3 hr, the wild type CcsBA shows two peaks of reduced heme, one at 560 nm and a 550 nm peak that is characteristic of covalent heme attached in c-type cytochromes.
source: Within 1–3 hr, the wt CcsBA shows two peaks of reduced heme, one at 560 nm and a 550 nm peak that is characteristic of covalent heme attached in c-type cytochromes (Figure 6c, red spectra).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Purified wild type CcsBA acts as a cytochrome c synthase in vitro and heme is attached from the P-His/WWD domain.
source: We conclude that purified wt CcsBA acts as a cyt c synthase in vitro and that heme is attached from the P-His/WWD domain, as hypothesized from in vivo results.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on in vitro data with wild type and P-His variant.

claim: The covalent attachment to apocytochrome c by CcsBA is measurable at 20 min, reaching a maximum at approximately 3 hr.
source: A time course of in vitro reactions with wt CcsBA shows that the covalent attachment to apocyt c is measurable at 20 min, reaching a maximum at approximately 3 hr (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6e.

claim: CcsBA in vitro synthesized cytochrome c is released and elutes at the same position as purified cytochrome c.
source: CcsBA in vitro synthesized cyt c is released and elutes at the same position as purified cyt c.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on HPLC data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Apocytochrome c is matured and released by CcsBA in vitro, with folding of cytochrome c into its native state.
source: We conclude that apocyt c is matured and released by CcsBA in vitro, with folding of cyt c into its native state.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on HPLC and spectral data.

claim: In CcsBA in vitro reactions, the 20mer, 16mer, and 11mer peptides each resulted in covalent heme after 3 hr.
source: In CcsBA in vitro reactions, the 20mer, 16mer, and 11mer peptides each resulted in covalent heme after 3 hr in vitro reactions (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The 56mer and 9mer were also recognized and attached to heme by CcsBA.
source: The 56mer (alpha helix 1 and 2 of cyt c) and 9mer were also recognized and attached to heme by CcsBA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bacterial CcsBA cytochrome c synthase does not require the alpha helix 1 and the recognition requirements are different than the mitochondrial HCCS.
source: We conclude that the bacterial CcsBA cyt c synthase does not require the alpha helix 1 and that the recognition requirements are different than the mitochondrial HCCS (see Figure 7—figure supplement 2 for parallel reactions of HCCS and CcsBA.)
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on comparative peptide experiments.

claim: All substitutions were recognized by HCCS, having at least a single thioether, with the exception of the SXXSH variant.
source: In the case of HCCS, all 20mer peptide variants possessed at least one covalent attachment with the exception of the SXXSH variant (Table 1, blue highlights).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and summarized in Table 1.

claim: HCCS does not require both cysteines for recognition.
source: This indicates that HCCS does not require both cysteines for recognition, a conclusion consistent with in vivo results of engineered cyt c substrate variants (Babbitt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on cysteine substitution experiments and cited in vivo work.

claim: For CcsBA, only one 20mer cysteine variant showed any covalent attachment: the first cysteine thiol replaced with a homocysteine.
source: In the case of the bacterial CcsBA, an entirely different set of rules emerge for CXXCH substrate recognition (Table 1, compare blue to orange highlighted variants). Only one 20mer cysteine variant showed any covalent attachment: the first cysteine thiol replaced with a homocysteine (Figure 7—figure supplement 3f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3f and Table 1.

claim: The HoCys15 variant has two covalent linkages (550 nm peak), suggesting that the first thiol is more permissive in distance from the alpha carbon for CcsBA.
source: The HoCys15 variant has two covalent linkages (550 nm peak), suggesting that the first thiol is more permissive in distance from the alpha carbon (i.e. of the first cysteine of CXXCH).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on spectral data.

claim: No 20mers with histidine substitutions possess covalently attached heme with CcsBA.
source: No 20mers with histidine substitutions possess covalently attached heme with CcsBA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: No protein factors other than the cytochrome c synthases are necessary for attachment and folding into a native cytochrome c structure in vitro.
source: Besides DTT for maintaining a reducing environment, no accessory factors other than HCCS and CcsBA are necessary. In vitro reactions result in stereochemical heme attachment, release of cyt c from the synthases, and proper folding into its native cyt c conformation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a major finding of the study.

claim: The cytochrome c produced in vitro possesses His19 (of CXXCH) and Met81 as axial ligands.
source: The cyt c possesses His19 (of CXXCH) and Met81 as axial ligands and its redox potential is identical to native cyt c purified from mitochondria (+253 mV).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the characterization of the in vitro product.

claim: The redox potential of in vitro produced cytochrome c is identical to native cytochrome c purified from mitochondria (+253 mV).
source: The cyt c possesses His19 (of CXXCH) and Met81 as axial ligands and its redox potential is identical to native cyt c purified from mitochondria (+253 mV).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the characterization of the in vitro product.

claim: A 20mer peptide with CXXCH is very poorly released by HCCS, thus halting the process after step 3.
source: In vitro reactions with HCCS and apocyt c proceed through all four steps (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), including step 4, release with cyt c folding. However, a 20mer peptide with CXXCH is very poorly released by HCCS, thus halting the process after step 3.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on release assay data.

claim: Single cysteine variants of cytochrome c (CXXCH motif) are released less than the wild type cytochrome c from HCCS in vivo.
source: In vivo we have demonstrated that single cysteine variants of cyt c (CXXCH motif) are released less than the wt cyt c, since more HCCS/cyt c complex and less cyt c product is purified (Babbitt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous in vivo work.

claim: Thioether formation and consequent heme distortion contributes to release of cytochrome c from HCCS.
source: We proposed that thioether formation and consequent heme distortion contributes to release.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Peptides with two thioethers release more than those with single thioethers from HCCS.
source: Using cysteine peptide variants, we demonstrate in vitro that peptides with two thioethers release more than those with the single thioethers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Full cytochrome c is released at least 62 ± 5%, 20mer 14 ± 3%, and the SXXCH variant 5 ± 2% from HCCS.
source: Full cyt c is released at least 62 ± 5%, 20mer 14 ± 3%, and the SXXCH variant 5 ± 2% from HCCS.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing release data.

claim: For CcsBA, biogenesis involves heme trafficking from an internal membrane site, liganded by two TM-His residues, to an external domain called the WWD/P-His site.
source: For CcsBA, we have proposed that biogenesis involves heme trafficking from an internal membrane site, liganded by two TM-His residues, to an external domain called the WWD/P-His site (Figure 6a, Frawley and Kranz, 2009; Sutherland et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work and reference to a figure.

claim: Heme from the WWD/P-His site is stereochemically attached to apocytochrome c (CXXCH) by CcsBA.
source: Subsequently, it is proposed that heme from the WWD/P-His site is stereochemically attached to apocyt c (CXXCH) (Sutherland et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Preliminary data on the spectral properties of peptides with heme attached by CcsBA appear to be released, unlike HCCS.
source: Preliminary data on the spectral properties of peptides with heme attached by CcsBA appear to be released, unlike HCCS.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a preliminary observation.

claim: The highly conserved WWD domain in the bacterial synthase may mediate release of heme-attached peptides.
source: Perhaps this release is mediated by the highly conserved WWD domain in the bacterial synthase, which interfaces with the edge of heme that faces the CXXCH substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The substrate requirements for HCCS and CcsBA are quite different.
source: In vitro reconstitution with CXXCH peptides and analogs have shown that the substrate requirements for HCCS and CcsBA are quite different.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a major finding from peptide experiments.

claim: HCCS only recognizes and attaches heme to the 16 and 20mer but not the 11mer or a 9mer, while CcsBA attaches to all four peptides.
source: HCCS only recognizes and attaches heme to the 16 and 20mer but not the 11mer or a 9mer, while CcsBA attaches to all four peptides (Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The alpha helix 1 sequence is predicted by PEP-FOLD to form an alpha helix, consistent with experimental structure of cytochrome c.
source: Structure of this alpha helix 1 sequence is predicted by PEP-FOLD (Shen et al., 2014; Thévenet et al., 2012) to form an alpha helix, consistent with experimental structure of cytochrome c.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to the prediction method.

claim: The alpha helix 1 is a critical component recognized by HCCS, and these peptides (16 and 20mers) present necessary and sufficient structures for recognition.
source: We conclude that the alpha helix 1 is a critical component recognized by HCCS, and that these peptides (16 and 20mers) present necessary and sufficient structures for recognition (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from peptide experiments.

claim: A Gremlin co-evolution/Rosetta approach was used to determine the structure of HCCS.
source: We used a Gremlin co-evolution/Rosetta approach (Ovchinnikov et al., 2017; Ovchinnikov et al., 2015) to determine the structure of HCCS, facilitated by almost a billion years of HCCS evolution (Babbitt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to the methods.

claim: The surface at the proposed active site of HCCS is acidic, potentially interacting electrostatically with the basic features of alpha helix 1.
source: The surface at the proposed active site of HCCS is acidic (Figure 8a), potentially interacting electrostatically with the basic features of alpha helix 1 (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: During step 2 of proposed model for HCCS function, His19 of apocytochrome c forms the second axial ligand to heme at the HCCS active site.
source: Moreover, during step 2 of proposed model for HCCS function (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), His19 of apocyt c forms the second axial ligand to heme at the HCCS active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to a figure showing the model.

claim: In all peptides with alpha helix 1, spectral analysis indicated that His 19 formed the second axial ligand.
source: In all peptides with alpha helix 1, spectral analysis indicated that His 19 formed this second axial ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on spectral data.

claim: Only the H19M variant showed a low amount of attached heme, with a spectrum that also implies methionine can replace the weak ligand in HCCS.
source: We have confirmed the requirement for His19, testing three His19 variants of the 20mer peptide, H19M, H19A, and H19K (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Only the H19M variant showed a low amount of attached heme, with a spectrum that also implies methionine can replace the weak ligand in HCCS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changing all basic lysines to aspartates in alpha helix 1 resulted in no heme attachment by HCCS, suggesting that the positive charge in alpha helix 1 is important.
source: For example, to test the electrostatic hypothesis, we changed all basic lysines to aspartates, retaining a predicted alpha helix 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1). Heme was not attached to this peptide by HCCS, suggesting that the positive charge in alpha helix 1 is important.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: For CcsBA, a limited sequence that includes CXXCH is necessary and sufficient.
source: For CcsBA, a limited sequence that includes CXXCH is necessary and sufficient.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from peptide experiments.

claim: Results using peptide analogs with non-standard thiol amino acids are consistent with a more stringent requirement for the CXXCH motif for CcsBA.
source: Results using peptide analogs with non-standard thiol amino acids are consistent with a more stringent requirement for the CXXCH motif for CcsBA.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on cysteine substitution experiments.

claim: Because bacteria often recognize hundreds of c-type cytochromes (i.e. CXXCH motifs) it makes evolutionary sense to recognize only the CXXCH motif, than to have a more demanding three-dimensional structure.
source: In this respect, because bacteria often recognize hundreds of c-type cytochromes (i.e. CXXCH motifs) it makes evolutionary sense to recognize only the CXXCH motif, than to have a more demanding three-dimensional structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an evolutionary interpretation.

claim: For HCCS, the only thiol amino acid analog with a thioether was d-cysteine substituted for the first cysteine (20mer DCys15).
source: For HCCS, the only thiol amino acid analog with a thioether was d-cysteine substituted for the first cysteine (20mer DCys15 in Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Table 1.

claim: For HCCS, there is some rotational flexibility at the first thiol, but no 'vertical' flexibility since the homocysteine at Cys15 did not form a thioether.
source: This suggests some rotational flexibility at the first thiol, but no 'vertical' flexibility since the homocysteine at Cys15 did not form a thioether.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the cysteine substitution data.

claim: For CcsBA, since only the homocysteine at Cys15 was attached, it may possess less rotational flexibility but more 'vertical' flexibility at the first cysteine at its active site.
source: In contrast, for CcsBA, since only the homocysteine at Cys15 was attached, it may possess less rotational flexibility but more 'vertical' flexibility at the first cysteine at its active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the cysteine substitution data.

claim: In spite of the commonly proposed universal CXXCH motif for all c-type cytochromes, the bacterial and mitochondrial cytochrome c synthases have evolved quite different recognition determinants and thus, mechanisms.
source: It is remarkable that in spite of the commonly proposed universal CXXCH motif for all c-type cytochromes, the bacterial and mitochondrial cyt c synthases have evolved quite different recognition determinants and thus, mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a major conclusion of the study.

claim: The different recognition requirements of bacterial and mitochondrial synthases are likely due to the limited c-type cyts in mitochondria (i.e. cyt c/cyt c1) but the large repertoire of c-type cyts in bacteria.
source: As discussed above, this is likely due to the limited c-type cyts in mitochondria (i.e. cyt c/cyt c1) but the large repertoire of c-type cyts in bacteria, each possessing CXXCH, and sometimes dozens of CXXCH motifs in a single bacterial protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an evolutionary explanation.

claim: Peptides recognized by HCCS inhibit heme attachment to subsequently added cytochrome c.
source: Multiple approaches were used to demonstrate that CXXCH peptides with alpha helix one are not released by HCCS, with single cysteine substitutions even more tightly bound (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Evidence is presented that peptides recognized by HCCS inhibit heme attachment to subsequently added cyt c.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Tightly bound peptides that are not released may inhibit subsequent binding of new heme and cytochrome c substrates; thus, they act as substrate analog type inhibitors.
source: Second, in principle, tightly bound peptides that are not released may inhibit subsequent binding of new heme and cyt c substrates; thus, they act as substrate analog type inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed mechanism of inhibition.

claim: Specific inhibitors could constitute targeted antimicrobials, facilitating chemical control of cytochrome c levels in selected organisms.
source: Because bacteria and humans (mitochondria) use very different cyt c synthases, shown here to recognize distinct features of the CXXCH substrate, specific inhibitors could constitute targeted antimicrobials, facilitating chemical control of cyt c levels in selected organisms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a potential application of the findings.
